opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it's one where the field is still sorting out its intuitions.

Predicting future sensor data in very high detail, whether that's camera pixels or full lidar point clouds, is very compelling. It's a self-supervised signal, so you can train on enormous amounts of driving data without labels. And if you can generate realistic sensor streams, you get a powerful simulator: you can create scenarios, vary them, and test the full stack end to end, including perception. That's real value, and we take it seriously.

But I'd separate two things: how well a model *renders* the world and how well it *understands* it. A lot of the capacity in a high-fidelity sensor model goes into things that don't matter much for driving: the texture of the asphalt, exactly how leaves move, reflections on a building. What matters for decisions is a much more compact set of factors. Where are the agents? What are they likely to do? How will they react to me? What's the road structure? What's occluded and what might be hiding there? A model can produce beautiful video and still be wrong or inconsistent on exactly those things, especially in the long tail.

So for me the question is always what you're using the model for. If the goal is closed-loop simulation and evaluation of the full system, sensor-level fidelity matters, because perception is part of what you're testing. Even then, what you need is controllability and consistency. The scene should respond correctly when the ego vehicle does something different, objects should persist, physics should hold up. Pretty pixels that drift over a few seconds don't help you validate safety.

If the goal is planning or reasoning about behavior, I lean toward more abstract, structured representations. Objects, maps, and intent are where the decision-relevant information lives, and they're much cheaper to roll forward and reason over. I think the sweet spot is often a hybrid: learn rich representations from raw sensor data, which is where the self-supervised signal really helps, but do the prediction and imagination of the future in a latent or structured space that's tuned to what the driver actually needs.

Then there's scale and cost. High-detail generation is expensive. If you want to simulate billions of miles or evaluate many variations of a rare scenario, you have to decide where to spend that compute. Usually you want high fidelity where it matters and cheaper abstractions everywhere else.

So I value high-fidelity world models a lot, but as one tool in a hierarchy, not the end goal. The real measure is whether they help you build a safer driver and give you confidence that it's safe, not how realistic the video looks.

r001.rationale: The response says high-detail generation is expensive, but does not state that greater fidelity requires larger models to capture added nuance.

r002.rationale: It favors structured representations for planning and reasoning, but does not ask whether the model could predict driving actions directly instead of detailed sensor data.

r003.rationale: It discusses simulation scale and compute costs, but does not question whether driving improvements justify the pretraining compute for highly detailed world models.

r004.rationale: It names simulator construction and evaluation as valuable uses, but does not identify simulation as an independent reason regardless of world models' value for building the driver.

r005.rationale: It mentions evaluating the full system and validating safety, but does not distinguish evaluating performance across the required range of cases from building the driver.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a question we think about a lot, because there's a real temptation, when you see these really impressive generative video models, to say the goal of a world model is to render the future at full fidelity. And I'd push back on that a bit. The question I always ask is: what is the model for? A world model, for us, is a tool that serves a planner. It's supposed to help the vehicle reason about what's going to happen next and how its own actions change that. If you frame it that way, then predicting every pixel, every lidar return, every texture on the side of a building, is mostly wasted capacity. The vast majority of the bits in a sensor stream don't matter for the decision you have to make.

What does matter is the structure underneath: where are the agents, what are they likely to do, how do those futures depend on what I do, and how uncertain am I about all of that. That's actually a fairly low-dimensional thing compared to raw sensor data. So if I spend enormous amounts of model capacity and compute learning to reproduce the exact appearance of the world, I'm optimizing a loss that's only loosely aligned with driving well.

That said, I don't want to be too dismissive, because high-fidelity prediction has real value in a couple of places. One is as a learning signal. Predicting sensor data is a very rich self-supervised objective. You don't need labels, you have essentially unlimited data, and forcing a model to predict the future at a detailed level does teach it a lot about geometry, dynamics, occlusion, how agents behave. So as a pretraining objective, it's quite compelling. The other place is simulation. If I want to close the loop and test my full stack, including perception, on counterfactual scenarios, then I need something that produces realistic sensor inputs. There, fidelity is the point, not a side effect.

So the way I'd summarize it is: fidelity is instrumentally valuable, not intrinsically valuable. For training representations and for building simulators, yes, detail matters a lot. For the model that actually sits in the decision loop and has to run in real time, I'd much rather have a compact, well-calibrated model of the things that matter, with honest uncertainty, than a beautiful video of the future that's confidently wrong about whether the pedestrian steps off the curb.

r001.rationale: The candidate says detailed sensor prediction can consume enormous model capacity and compute, but does not clearly state that higher fidelity requires larger models to capture added nuance.

r002.rationale: It says the model should serve a planner and focus on decision-relevant structure, but does not ask whether the model could predict driving actions directly.

r003.rationale: The candidate contrasts detailed prediction with decision-aligned driving performance and notes compute costs, but does not specifically question whether driving improvements justify pretraining compute.

r004.rationale: It presents simulation as a separate use: realistic sensor inputs for testing the full stack on counterfactual scenarios, where fidelity is itself the goal.

r005.rationale: It mentions testing the full stack in simulation, but does not distinguish validating a driver's performance across the required range of cases from building the driver.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is, what do you need that prediction for? In autonomous driving, you want to understand how the scene could evolve and what that means for the actions you might take. A model that predicts future sensor data in great detail can be useful, but visual fidelity alone doesn’t tell you whether it captures the things that matter for driving.

For example, does it get the behavior of a pedestrian right? Does it capture how another driver might react if you start merging? Those are more consequential than whether it renders every texture correctly. And the future is uncertain, so you want plausible alternative outcomes, rather than one very detailed prediction that looks convincing.

I would evaluate that model by whether it helps us make better decisions or test the system more effectively. The detail is valuable insofar as it supports those goals.

r002.rationale: It mentions actions the driver might take, but does not ask whether the model could predict driving actions directly instead of sensor data.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss driving improvements in relation to pretraining compute costs.

r004.rationale: It does not identify simulator construction as an independent reason to develop world models.

r005.rationale: It mentions testing the system, but does not distinguish validating a driver's performance across required cases from building the driver.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is how much of that detail matters for driving. Predicting future sensor data is a very rich learning objective, and it can help you learn a lot about the structure of the world. But you can also spend a tremendous amount of capacity predicting things that have very little impact on the decisions the vehicle needs to make.

So I would evaluate it in terms of whether it helps us understand how the scene might evolve and choose better actions. Does it capture the behavior of other road users? Can it represent multiple plausible futures? And does it respond correctly when we change what our own vehicle does? A prediction can look very realistic without getting those interactions right. The detail is valuable insofar as it improves those capabilities and, ultimately, the driving.
